title: When the Visitor Breaks
premise: Ada Thornbury, a pest controller who survived a childhood haunting by refusing to acknowledge it, is called back to the house where 'the Visitor' once lived in the walls—only to find their imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on the porch, unchanged after twenty years. The Visitor doesn't haunt; it collects the children who sang its lullaby, and Ada only escaped because they never learned the last verse. Now every child from that street is disappearing one by one, and Wren claims the song can only be finished by someone who remembers how it started. To save the last surviving child, Ada must return to the nursery, learn the final verse without singing along, and offer the Visitor something it has never been given: recognition. In the end, Ada sings the verse silently, names the Visitor as what it truly was—a forgotten child like themselves—and breaks the cycle, though they lose Wren forever to do it.
about_author: Rafael Coldharbour is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade documenting empty houses across rural New England. Their fiction draws on maintenance logs, abandoned nurseries, and the quiet conviction that old houses remember being loved.

chapters.title: The Call Comes at Dusk
chapters.summary: Ada, nonbinary and guarded, takes a routine pest-control call to Hollowell Street—the street of their childhood. POV: Ada. The emotional beat is dread disguised as professionalism, as the address on the work order is their own childhood home.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Inside of the Glass
chapters.summary: Inspecting the empty Marlow house, Ada finds small handprints on windows—from the inside, too high for any child to reach. POV: Ada. The beat is the first crack in ten years of rational explanations.

chapters.title: Wren, Unchanged
chapters.summary: On the porch sits Wren, Ada's imaginary friend, exactly eight years old, exactly as remembered. Wren says: 'You left mid-song.' POV: Ada. The beat is vertigo—the past refusing to stay past.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter: young Ada surviving the hauntings by naming every noise—pipes, raccoons, settling beams—and refusing to sing the lullaby the other children hummed. POV: Ada (past). The beat is the price of survival: loneliness mistaken for safety.

chapters.title: The Missing List
chapters.summary: Ada researches and finds four adults from Hollowell Street have vanished this year, all former playmates, all children who sang. Wren confirms: the Visitor is finishing its collection. POV: Ada. The beat is guilt sharpening into responsibility.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Won't Say
chapters.summary: Ada interviews the last remaining resident, elderly Mrs. Okonkwo, who reveals the lullaby predates the neighborhood—it belongs to a child who died there in 1948. POV: Ada. The beat is horror acquiring a history.

chapters.title: The Song in the Walls
chapters.summary: Working alone at dusk, Ada hears the lullaby through the drywall, missing its final verse, looping. Their hands begin humming along involuntarily. POV: Ada. The beat is the body betraying the mind's defenses.

chapters.title: Rules of Not Singing
chapters.summary: Wren teaches Ada survival rules: never hum, never finish another's line, never answer when the song pauses. Each rule costs something human—a memory, a warmth. POV: Ada. The beat is belonging revealed as a trap dressed as comfort.

chapters.title: Danny's Empty Apartment
chapters.summary: Ada searches the apartment of Danny Reyes, the most recent disappearance, finding lyrics scrawled on every wall—the song complete, except the last verse, which is scratched out. POV: Ada. The beat is terror at evidence that someone tried and failed.

chapters.title: The Visitor's Shape
chapters.summary: Ada glimpses the Visitor at the edge of the nursery doorway: a silhouette made of every child's absence, wearing fingerprints like scales. POV: Ada. The beat is confrontation with the thing that has no explanation.

chapters.title: Why You Were Spared
chapters.summary: Wren confesses: Ada wasn't spared by silence—they were spared because the Visitor marked them as its own, an unfinished collection. Belonging was never optional. POV: Ada. The beat is identity collapsing: invisibility was always a cage.

chapters.title: Mrs. Okonkwo's Last Verse
chapters.summary: The dying Mrs. Okonkwo recalls half the final verse from her own childhood warning and gives Ada a recording before slipping into a song-induced sleep she won't wake from. POV: Ada. The beat is grief and urgency braided together.

chapters.title: Half a Verse Is Worse Than None
chapters.summary: Ada attempts the partial verse; the house responds violently, doors sealing, the Visitor nearly taking them. Wren pulls them out, diminished. POV: Ada. The beat is learning that incomplete knowledge is more dangerous than ignorance.

chapters.title: The Child of 1948
chapters.summary: In county archives Ada finds the death record: Edmund Vale, age seven, died alone in the house while the neighborhood sang elsewhere. The lullaby was his; no one ever finished singing it back to him. POV: Ada. The beat is pity displacing fear.

chapters.title: Wren's True Name
chapters.summary: Ada realizes Wren is not an imaginary friend but a previous taken child, sent back each generation as bait and messenger. Confronting them shatters their friendship. POV: Ada. The beat is betrayal and compassion in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Last Child
chapters.summary: The Visitor takes nine-year-old Priya, the final uncollected singer, into the nursery. Ada has until dawn. POV: Ada. The beat is the point of no return.

chapters.title: Into the Nursery
chapters.summary: Ada enters the sealed house at midnight, following the song downward into a nursery that shouldn't fit inside the house, wallpapered with decades of missing-person flyers. POV: Ada. The beat is descent—physical and moral.

chapters.title: The Collection
chapters.summary: Ada finds the missing adults suspended in the song, mouths moving, eyes open, alive but emptied. Among them, Danny mouths one word: 'finish.' POV: Ada. The beat is horror at survival worse than death.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: From Edmund's hidden diary, Ada reads the true final verse—not a summons but a plea to be found. They memorize it without voicing a sound. POV: Ada. The beat is understanding replacing strategy.

chapters.title: Singing Without Sound
chapters.summary: Climax: Ada stands before the Visitor and performs the verse in total silence—mouth shaping words, throat closed—naming Edmund, acknowledging him, refusing both to join and to flee. The Visitor fractures into a small, weeping boy. POV: Ada. The beat is courage as recognition, not violence.

chapters.title: Letting Wren Go
chapters.summary: The freed children wake, but Wren, sustained only by the cycle, begins to fade. Ada finally sings aloud—for Wren alone—as he dissolves, thanking them. POV: Ada. The beat is the cost of breaking the pattern: losing the only friend who stayed.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers Being Loved
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Ada seals the nursery, leaves flowers for Edmund, and watches Priya go home. On the porch, no one waits—and for the first time, that feels like peace rather than exile. POV: Ada. The beat is belonging redefined: chosen, not imposed.
